---
title: "Following evolution with the canonical equation"
subtitle: "Leaf mass per area and height at maturation evolving together in FF16"
format: html
---



[Finding evolutionary attractors](solving_attractors.qmd) locates the trait
values where selection stops by solving for a zero selection gradient. That
says where evolution can end, but not how it gets there, or whether it gets
there at all from a given start. The **canonical equation** of adaptive
dynamics follows the path [@Dieckmann-1996]. Each resident's traits move up
their selection gradient at a speed set by the supply of mutations:

$$
\frac{dz}{dt} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mu\,\tilde n\,V\,\nabla_z s(z),
$$

where $z$ are the traits on the scale the search uses (here the logarithm of
each trait), $\mu$ the mutation rate, $\tilde n$ the resident's equilibrium
density relative to the starting community's total, $V$ the mutational
covariance and $\nabla_z s$ the selection gradient. Time is measured in
units set by $\mu$, so only its relative values mean anything here. Every
evaluation of the right-hand side re-solves the community to demographic
equilibrium, so one evaluation costs one `plant` equilibrium plus one
selection gradient.

When every gradient vanishes, `regnans` checks each resident for a fitness
minimum. A resident at one branches, once a mutant that can invade and
coexist with it has had time to arise, and the equation carries on with both
lineages. Otherwise the run stops.

## Set up the community

Two traits evolve: leaf mass per area (`lma`) and height at maturation
(`hmat`). Patches last at most 30 years rather than the default 60, which
halves the cost of each `plant` run. The attractor depends on this choice.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(plant)
library(regnans)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

community0 <- community_start(
  bounds(lma = c(0.02, 0.6), hmat = c(2, 40)),
  model_support = list(
    p = plant_default_assembly_pars(max_patch_lifetime = 30),
    plant_control = plant_default_assembly_control()
  ),
  derivative_control = list(d_second = 1e-2)
)
```
:::


`d_second` is the relative step `regnans` uses for second derivatives. The
stepper below needs the Jacobian of the right-hand side, which `regnans`
finds by differencing selection gradients across equilibrium solves, and
each of those solves is converged to the cube of the step. A step of `1e-2`
needs solves only to `1e-6`, against `1e-9` at the default `1e-3`, and on
this problem reaches the same end point faster.

## Integrate the canonical equation

Start from thin, cheap leaves on a short plant (`lma = 0.15`, `hmat = 6`):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ce <- community_canonical_equation(
  community0,
  x0 = c(0.15, 6),
  control = canonical_control(list(stepper = "rodas"))
)

ce$outcome
#> [1] "stable"
ce$events
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>    time event  lineage
#>   <dbl> <chr>    <int>
#> 1 2823. polish      NA
#> 2 2823. stable      NA
```
:::


`stepper = "rodas"` is the default; it is written out here because it
matters. The two traits evolve on very different time scales: most of the
change in `lma` happens within a few units of evolutionary time, while
`hmat` takes thousands. A system like this is **stiff**. An explicit stepper
such as Cash–Karp (`"rkck"`) is held to steps short enough for the fast
`lma` direction long after `lma` has nearly stopped moving. In a trial
capped at 200 steps it had not arrived, after eight times the equilibrium
solves this run needs. RODAS, a linearly implicit stepper, takes steps as
long as the slow `hmat` direction allows, and gets there in 17.

As the gradients become small, the run finishes the approach by solving for
the stationary point directly (the `polish` event, which calls
`community_solve_singularity()`) rather than following an ever-slower
trajectory. `stable` means the run found no resident that could branch.

The end point:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
final <- ce$trajectory[nrow(ce$trajectory), ]
final[, c("time", "lma", "hmat", "density", "gradient_lma", "gradient_hmat")]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>    time    lma  hmat density gradient_lma gradient_hmat
#>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>        <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1 2823. 0.0473  10.9    37.9 -0.000000691      -4.86e-9
```
:::


To confirm what kind of point this is, rebuild the community there with
`canonical_community()` and classify it from its fitness Hessian and the
Jacobian of its selection gradient:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
end_community <- canonical_community(ce, final$time)
classification <- community_classify_singularity(end_community)
classification$classification
#> [1] "CSS"
```
:::


## The path

Over evolutionary time, `lma` falls quickly while `hmat` barely moves, and
`lma` dips a little below where it will end. Then `hmat` rises slowly, and
`lma` creeps back up as taller plants favour slightly denser leaves:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ce$trajectory |>
  pivot_longer(c(lma, hmat), names_to = "trait") |>
  ggplot(aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(vars(trait), scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(transform = "log1p", breaks = c(0, 1, 10, 100, 1000)) +
  labs(x = "Evolutionary time", y = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](canonical_equation_files/figure-html/path-time-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Seen in trait space, the path is an L. The points are the start, each
accepted step of the stepper, and the polished end point:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(ce$trajectory, aes(lma, hmat)) +
  geom_path() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  geom_point(data = final, colour = "red", size = 3) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Leaf mass per area, lma", y = "Height at maturation, hmat")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](canonical_equation_files/figure-html/path-space-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The red point is the end point classified above. Solving for it directly,
as [Finding evolutionary attractors](solving_attractors.qmd) describes, finds
where selection stops. The canonical equation adds the route there, and
whether evolution from this start reaches it.
